learn.title: Solar PV and the Photoelectric Effect
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels are key to transitioning away from fossil fuels. They convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect, a phenomenon discovered over a century ago. Understanding how they work helps us appreciate one of the most scalable and sustainable energy technologies driving global decarbonization.
learn.c1_text: When sunlight hits a solar panel, it knocks electrons loose from silicon atoms in the PV cells. This is the photoelectric effect—light energy transfers to electrons, allowing them to flow as electric current. Think of it like wind pushing sailboats: sunlight pushes electrons through wires to power your home.
learn.c2_text: Each solar cell has two layers of silicon—one positively doped (with phosphorus) and one negatively doped (with boron). When photons strike the junction, they create an electric field that pushes electrons toward the negative side, generating direct current (DC). An inverter then converts DC into alternating current (AC) for household use.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 3rd globally in solar capacity with over 75 GW installed by 2024. The International Solar Alliance, launched by India, aims to mobilize $1 trillion in solar investments globally. Large parks like Bhadla in Rajasthan showcase how solar farms can power millions of homes efficiently.
learn.stat2: Global solar capacity grew by 22% annually since 2010
learn.stat3: A typical residential solar system offsets 5–6 tons of CO₂ per year
learn.stat4: Silicon solar cells have an average efficiency of 15–22%

learn.title: Tidal Stream Energy Explained
learn.intro: Tidal stream energy captures the motion of ocean currents to generate clean electricity. Unlike solar or wind, tides are highly predictable, offering reliable baseload power. As coastal nations seek stable renewable sources, tidal energy presents a unique opportunity to harness Earth’s most consistent natural force.
learn.c1_text: Tidal streams are underwater currents caused by gravitational forces from the moon and sun. These flows can reach speeds up to 5 m/s, containing immense kinetic energy. Turbines placed in these currents spin like underwater windmills, converting motion into electricity with minimal visual impact on coastlines.
learn.c2_text: Tidal turbines resemble robust wind turbines designed for marine environments. They’re anchored to the seabed and often feature biplane or ducted designs to maximize energy capture. Because water is 800 times denser than air, even slow-moving tides can produce significant power output compared to airborne wind systems.
learn.c3_text: India’s 7,517 km coastline holds vast tidal energy potential, especially along the Bay of Bengal. Pilot projects in Tamil Nadu and Kerala are exploring feasibility. With strong monsoon-driven currents and government support under the National Offshore Wind Energy Policy, India could lead Asia in early tidal adoption.
learn.stat1: India: 7,517 km coastline suitable for tidal energy
learn.stat3: Tidal currents are predictable up to 100 years in advance
learn.stat4: One tidal turbine can power 600–1,000 homes annually

learn.title: Understanding Levelised Cost of Energy
learn.intro: The Levelised Cost of Energy (LCOE) is the average price a power source must charge to cover all its lifetime costs. It allows fair comparisons between solar farms, coal plants, and wind turbines. As renewables drop in cost, LCOE reveals how solar and wind now beat fossil fuels in many regions—reshaping investment decisions worldwide.
learn.c1_text: LCOE calculates total project cost divided by total energy produced over its lifetime. For example, if a solar farm costs $1 million and generates 2,000 MWh over 25 years, its LCOE is $0.50/kWh. This metric includes construction, operation, maintenance, and financing—but excludes subsidies or taxes.
learn.c2_text: Investors use LCOE to compare technologies fairly. Onshore wind might cost $0.03–$0.05/kWh, while utility-scale solar ranges $0.03–$0.06/kWh. In contrast, new coal plants range from $0.06–$0.14/kWh. Lower LCOE means cheaper electricity and faster return on investment, making renewables increasingly attractive.
learn.c3_text: Between 2010 and 2023, India’s solar LCOE fell by over 80%, reaching around ₹2.44/kWh (~$0.03/kWh). Wind costs dropped similarly due to better turbine tech and competitive auctions. These trends helped India attract $15 billion in renewable energy investments in FY2023 alone, accelerating its clean energy goals.
learn.stat2: Global utility-scale solar LCOE fell 86% from 2010 to 2022
learn.stat4: New coal-fired LCOE ranges from $0.06–$0.14/kWh worldwide

learn.title: India's ISTS Waiver Policy Impact
learn.intro: India’s Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) waiver policy allows renewable projects to sell power outside their bidding state without transmission charges. Introduced in 2014, it boosted competition and lowered tariffs. By removing regional barriers, the policy accelerated India’s renewable energy boom and attracted record foreign investment.
learn.c1_text: Before ISTS waivers, developers were limited to selling within their own states, often leading to oversupply or low demand. Now, solar and wind projects can connect anywhere on the national grid and sell to distant buyers. This flexibility increased market access and enabled aggressive tariff bidding in central auctions.
learn.c2_text: After introducing ISTS waivers, solar tariffs in India crashed from ₹12/kWh in 2014 to below ₹2/kWh by 2020. Wind tariffs followed suit. Developers could now compete nationally, driving efficiency and scale. The policy also encouraged hybrid projects combining solar and wind, improving grid stability and returns.
learn.c3_text: Thanks to ISTS waivers, India added over 175 GW of renewable capacity by 2024—exceeding targets. Major developers like ReNew Power and Adani Green expanded rapidly across states. The policy remains critical for meeting India’s net-zero by 2070 goal, enabling seamless integration of variable renewables into the national grid.
learn.stat1: India: 175 GW renewable capacity added by 2024
learn.stat3: Over 40 GW of solar projects commissioned under ISTS waiver scheme
learn.stat4: Foreign investment inflows into Indian renewables hit $15 billion in FY2023

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements Explained
learn.intro: A Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) is a long-term contract where a renewable energy developer sells electricity to a buyer at a fixed rate. PPAs provide revenue certainty, helping developers secure loans and investors. They’re vital for financing solar farms and wind parks, ensuring stable returns while locking in low electricity prices for buyers.
learn.c1_text: Imagine signing a 20-year lease to buy apples from an orchard at a set price each year. That’s a PPA—but for electrons. Buyers gain predictable energy costs; sellers get guaranteed income to fund construction. Banks see lower risk, so loans come easier. This model powers much of today’s renewable expansion.
learn.c2_text: Companies like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft sign corporate PPAs to meet sustainability goals. They agree to buy clean energy directly from wind or solar farms, often at rates cheaper than grid power. These deals help fund new projects and give corporations 24/7 renewable energy without owning infrastructure.
learn.c3_text: Indian firms like Tata Motors and Dalmia Cement have signed PPAs for hundreds of megawatts. The government’s waiver on inter-state transmission duties for solar projects boosted corporate interest. With falling tariffs and rising ESG focus, India expects 20 GW of corporate renewable PPAs by 2030.
learn.stat1: India targets 20 GW of corporate renewable PPAs by 2030
learn.stat2: Corporate PPAs globally reached 37 GW in 2022
learn.stat3: PPAs typically last 15–25 years with fixed pricing
learn.stat4: Over 60% of new U.S. wind capacity funded through PPAs in 2023

learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage Basics
learn.intro: Pumped hydro storage acts like a giant rechargeable battery, storing excess electricity by pumping water uphill and releasing it when needed. It provides over 90% of global energy storage capacity, balancing supply and demand on the grid. As variable renewables grow, pumped hydro ensures reliable, dispatchable power whenever the sun doesn’t shine or wind doesn’t blow.
learn.c1_text: Think of it like filling a bucket from a tank above—you store potential energy. During surplus periods, excess electricity pumps water from a lower reservoir to an upper one. When demand spikes, water flows down through turbines, generating electricity in minutes. One facility can store enough energy to power thousands of homes for hours.
learn.c2_text: Pumped hydro responds within seconds to grid signals, making it ideal for frequency regulation and peak shaving. A single plant like Bath County in Virginia can generate 3 GW instantly—enough for 750,000 homes. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, it lasts decades and scales economically to hundreds of GWh.
learn.c3_text: India operates over 4.5 GW of pumped hydro storage with plans to add 10 GW by 2030. Projects like Koel-Karo in Jharkhand aim to support renewable integration. Given India’s growing solar and wind fleet, pumped hydro will play a crucial role in maintaining grid stability and reducing curtailment of green energy.

learn.stat2: Pumped hydro supplies over 90% of global energy storage
learn.stat3: Bath County Pumped Storage: 3 GW capacity in the U.S.
learn.stat4: India currently operates 4.5 GW of pumped hydro storage
